## Introduction

The goal of this lab was to build a simple Internet of Things (IoT) device. An ESP8266 WiFi
module hosts a web page that lets a user turn an LED on and off and view the current room
temperature. The STM32L432KC MCU does the real work:

- It receives web requests from the ESP8266 over a **125000 baud UART** link.
- It toggles the LED on `PA6`.
- It reads the temperature from a **DS1722 digital thermometer over SPI**, using an SPI driver
  I wrote with the CMSIS device templates in `stm32l432xx.h`.
- It generates the HTML page and sends it back to the ESP8266, which forwards it to the browser.

Beyond the required LED control and temperature display, the web page also lets the user change
the sensor's resolution from 8 to 12 bits. The temperature is displayed with as many decimal
places as the selected resolution provides.

## Design and Testing Methodology

The GPIO, RCC, FLASH, TIM, and USART libraries and the ESP8266 web server code come from the
Lab 6 starter code. I wrote the SPI driver (`STM32L432KC_SPI.c/h`), the DS1722 driver
(`DS1722.c/h`), and the request handling and web page generation in `main.c`.

### ESP8266–MCU interface

The ESP8266 is connected to `USART1` on the MCU, with TX and RX crossed: MCU TX (`PA9`) goes to
ESP RX and MCU RX (`PA10`) goes to ESP TX. Each time a browser loads the page, the ESP8266 sends
the most recent request as `/REQ:<tag>\n` (for example, `/REQ:ledon\n`). The main loop:

1. Reads characters from the UART until it sees `\n`.
2. Checks the request for a resolution tag (`res8` to `res12`) and reconfigures the DS1722 if
   one is present.
3. Reads the temperature over SPI.
4. Checks the request for `ledon` / `ledoff` and drives `PA6`.
5. Sends the full HTML page, from `<!DOCTYPE html>` to `</html>`, back over the UART.

When checking for resolution tags, the two-digit tags (`res10`, `res11`, `res12`) are tested
before `res8`/`res9`, so a request is never matched to the wrong resolution.

### SPI driver

`initSPI(br, cpol, cpha)` configures `SPI1` directly through its memory-mapped registers:

- **Pins:** `SCK` on `PB3`, `MISO` on `PB4` and `MOSI` on `PB5`, all set to alternate
  function 5. The chip enable `CE` on `PB1` is a regular GPIO output, because the DS1722's chip
  enable is **active high**, unlike the active-low NSS of the SPI peripheral.
- **`CR1`:** master mode, software slave management (`SSM`, `SSI`), MSB first, and the baud
  rate, polarity, and phase passed in as arguments.
- **`CR2`:** 8-bit data size (`DS = 0b0111`) with `FRXTH` set, so `RXNE` flags after a single byte.

The DS1722 is initialized with `initSPI(0b111, 0, 1)`:

- `BR = 0b111` divides the 80 MHz clock by 256, giving a **312.5 kHz SCK**, well under the
  DS1722's 5 MHz maximum.
- `CPOL = 0, CPHA = 1` matches the DS1722 SPI timing, where data changes on the rising edge of
  SCK and is sampled on the falling edge.

`spiSendReceive()` waits for `TXE`, writes one byte to `DR`, waits for `RXNE`, and returns the
received byte. `DR` is accessed through an 8-bit pointer so that each write sends exactly one
byte rather than packing two.

### DS1722 driver

Every DS1722 transaction is two bytes inside one chip-enable window: an address byte followed
by a data byte.

| Function | Address | Data | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `initDS1722(res)` | `0x80` (config write) | `0xE0 + ((res − 8) << 1)` | Continuous conversion at the selected resolution |
| `readTempRaw()` | `0x02` (temp MSB) | `0x00` (dummy) | Integer part, °C (two's complement) |
| | `0x01` (temp LSB) | `0x00` (dummy) | Fractional part, in 1/16 °C steps at 12-bit |

`readTempRaw()` combines the two bytes into a signed 16-bit value. The temperature in °C is then
`raw / 256`.

### Testing

1. **SPI without the sensor.** Before wiring the DS1722, I probed `CE`, `SCK`, `MOSI` and `MISO`
   with the logic analyzer. I checked that the configuration write and the temperature reads
   produced the right addresses, data, clock polarity and phase, and chip-enable framing.
2. **SPI with the sensor.** With the DS1722 connected, I decoded the MISO bytes from the scope
   captures and compared them to the temperature shown on the web page.
3. **Web page.** I connected to the ESP8266's access point, loaded `http://192.168.4.1/`, and
   checked that the LED buttons toggled the LED and its status text, and that each resolution
   button changed the number of decimal places shown.

### Schematic

<!-- TODO: add the schematic, e.g.
![Figure 2: Schematic of the MCU, ESP8266, DS1722 and LED.](images/lab6_schematic.jpg){width=90% fig-align="center"}
-->

The DS1722 is powered from 3.3 V, with its `SERMODE` pin tied high to select SPI mode. `CE`,
`SCLK`, `SDI` and `SDO` connect to `PB1`, `PB3`, `PB5` (MOSI) and `PB4` (MISO). The ESP8266 is
powered from 3.3 V and connects to `PA9`/`PA10`. The LED is driven from `PA6` through a
current-limiting resistor. The DIP switches between the MCU and the FPGA are open, so the FPGA
cannot drive any of these pins.

### SPI logic analyzer captures

In each capture, channel 1 (yellow) is `CE`, 2 (green) is `SCK`, 3 (blue) is `MISO`, and
4 (pink) is `MOSI`.

## Results and Discussion

![Figure 9: The web page served by the ESP8266, showing the LED status and a 12-bit temperature reading of 23.1875 °C.](images/Lab6_Webpage.png){width=90% fig-align="center"}

The device works as intended. Loading `http://192.168.4.1/` shows the LED controls, the LED
status, the current temperature, and the resolution buttons. Clicking *Turn the LED on!* or
*Turn the LED off!* changes both the LED and its status text. The temperature reads about 23 °C,
a reasonable room temperature.

The logic analyzer captures confirm the SPI timing: `CE` stays high for the whole two-byte
transaction, data changes on the rising edge of `SCK`, and the sensor's MISO bytes match the
temperature on the web page.

The ESP8266 is slow, so a page sometimes takes a few seconds or a couple of reloads to appear.
Also, because the page is only regenerated when it is requested, the temperature updates only
when the page is refreshed or a button is clicked.

The design meets all of the proficiency requirements. The adjustable-resolution controls go
beyond the base specification.

## Conclusion

The STM32L432KC parses web requests from the ESP8266 over UART, controls an LED, reads the DS1722
over a CMSIS-based SPI driver, and serves a dynamic HTML page with the LED state and the current
temperature at a user-selectable resolution.
